column1: Create a view with {{c1::CREATE VIEW}} Sales.ActiveCustomers AS SELECT CustomerID, CustomerName FROM Sales.Customers WHERE IsActive = 1;
column2:
This stores a reusable definition for the active-customer query. The ordinary view does not store a separate copy of the customer rows.
Review source

column1: Define a view's query with CREATE VIEW Sales.CustomerNames {{c1::AS}} SELECT CustomerID, CustomerName FROM Sales.Customers;
column2:
AS introduces the SELECT that defines the view. The listed fields become the view's exposed columns.
Review source

column1: A view can hide a reusable {{c1::JOIN}} between customer and order tables behind one queryable object.
column2:
Define the customer and order relationship once inside the view. A report can select from the view without rewriting its join.
Review source

column1: A view can calculate an order category with {{c1::CASE}} WHEN TotalAmount < 100 THEN 'Small' ELSE 'Other' END AS OrderSize.
column2:
CASE classifies each row based on its amount. The alias lets callers refer to the result as OrderSize.
Review source

column1: A calculated expression exposed by a view needs a {{c1::column name}}, supplied by an alias or the view's column list.
column2:
SQL Server needs a name for each output column. Unlike an ordinary column reference, a calculated expression has no source column name to inherit.
Review source

column1: For an updatable filtered view, place {{c1::WITH CHECK OPTION}} after the SELECT query to enforce visibility after INSERT or UPDATE.
column2:
The option applies the filter to rows inserted or updated through the view. It rejects a write that would leave the row outside the filtered result.
Review source

column1: An otherwise valid INSERT of TotalAmount = 500 through a view filtered by TotalAmount > 1000 WITH CHECK OPTION is {{c1::rejected}}.
column2:
An amount of 500 does not satisfy the filter of greater than 1000. The option rejects the INSERT instead of allowing an immediately hidden row.
Review source

column1: WITH CHECK OPTION tests writes made {{c1::through the view}} rather than direct writes to the tables.
column2:
A direct update to the table does not use this view and therefore does not run its visibility test. A table constraint can enforce a rule across entry points.
Review source

column1: To use a view as a restricted data interface, grant access to it while restricting direct access to {{c1::its base tables}}.
column2:
Access through the view alone limits callers to its definition. A separate permission on a source table can expose data the view omits.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, the first index that materializes a view must be a {{c1::unique clustered index}}.
column2:
The unique clustered index is what stores the view result. Schema binding is a prerequisite but does not materialize the result by itself.
Review source

column1: Indexed views can increase base-table write costs because SQL Server must also {{c1::maintain the views' stored results}}.
column2:
Base-table changes must update the view index in the same operation. Consider whether faster reads justify those extra writes.
Review source

column1: To guarantee sorted results when querying a SQL Server view, put ORDER BY in {{c1::the outer SELECT query}}.
column2:
Only the caller's ORDER BY guarantees the requested output order. An order inside a view can affect which rows TOP selects without sorting the caller's result.
Review source
